title: Broad wellbeing remains moderate while loneliness, anxiety, and material issue salience stay unevenly distributed by age
source_unit: Office for National Statistics, Public opinions and social trends, Great Britain: personal wellbeing and loneliness, 5 to 30 August 2026
geography: Great Britain; adults responding to the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN)

denominator.unit: Great Britain adults in the life-satisfaction item; item-specific OPN samples vary

anxiety_all.unit: mean score from 0 to 10, where higher means more anxious

wellbeing_not_one_score.value: Moderate broad wellbeing can coexist with elevated anxiety and loneliness; a single life-satisfaction score hides the pattern

observations.method: Weighted OPN estimates with published confidence intervals and item-specific sample sizes; means are reported separately for personal wellbeing measures.
observations.uncertainty: The survey is repeated cross-sectional rather than a panel, and self-reported means do not establish causes or clinical mental-health prevalence. Age comparisons should be read with their confidence intervals and differing item bases.
observations.subgroup: All persons and adults aged 16 to 29.
observations.counterinterpretation: Near-similar young and all-person means may indicate resilience or measurement compression rather than equal lived conditions; anxiety and loneliness capture different dimensions from life satisfaction.

observations.period: 5 to 30 August 2026; low and high wellbeing thresholds

denominator.unit: Great Britain adults; threshold item bases vary

high_anxiety_young.unit: percent of age 16 to 29 with high anxiety

high_hope_young.unit: percent of age 16 to 29 with high hope

threshold_split.value: Young adults show both high hope and slightly higher high-anxiety prevalence, making aspiration and distress coexisting rather than mutually exclusive categories

observations.method: ONS threshold classifications derived from the same OPN wellbeing battery; estimates include lower and upper confidence limits in the source workbook.
observations.uncertainty: Thresholds are operational classifications, not diagnoses or stable individual trajectories; the August 2026 workbook also records a correction to a July 2026 Table 24 estimate, so historical extracts should be version-controlled.
observations.subgroup: All persons and adults aged 16 to 29.
observations.counterinterpretation: The apparent coexistence of hope and anxiety may reflect different questions, timing, or subgroups rather than a single psychological state.

observations.period: 5 to 30 August 2026; loneliness and long-run rolling trend

denominator.unit: Great Britain adults answering the loneliness item

rolling_trend.value: The latest 25% estimate is within the broad 2020-2026 rolling range, with repeated recent estimates mostly between 23% and 27%

loneliness_age_gradient.value: Loneliness is more concentrated among younger adults than older age bands in this period

observations.method: OPN responses to a self-reported loneliness frequency question; the workbook provides all-person trend estimates from March 2020 and current age-band breakdowns.
observations.uncertainty: The rolling periods are repeated cross-sections, not a panel; the time-series range is descriptive and should not be interpreted as a causal pandemic or post-pandemic effect. Loneliness is not a clinical diagnosis.
observations.subgroup: All persons, age 16 to 29, 30 to 49, 50 to 69, 70 and over, and sex groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Age differences may reflect life stage, household composition, reporting norms, survey coverage, or exposure to other forms of social contact rather than age itself.

observations.period: 5 to 30 August 2026; important issues by age

denominator.unit: OPN respondents; issue-specific sample sizes and confidence intervals are published in the workbook

cost_of_living_all.unit: percent naming cost of living as an important issue

housing_young.unit: percent of age 16 to 29 naming housing

immigration_young_vs_older.value: 42% of age 16 to 29 versus 82% of age 70 and over

international_conflict_young_vs_older.value: 39% of age 16 to 29 versus 60% of age 70 and over

issue_salience_mechanism.value: Material pressures are near-universal, but housing is especially age-sensitive and geopolitical/identity issues are strongly age-stratified

observations.method: OPN question asking respondents which issues face the UK, with all-person and age-band percentages and confidence intervals.
observations.uncertainty: Issue selection is salience, not ranked policy preference or causal concern; respondents can select multiple issues. Age patterns may be shaped by life stage, media exposure, and question interpretation.
observations.subgroup: All persons and age bands 16 to 29, 30 to 49, 50 to 69, and 70 and over.
observations.counterinterpretation: High material issue salience does not imply that cultural or geopolitical concerns are absent; salience can reflect immediate household exposure and available public language for describing insecurity.

related_sources.claim: ONS wellbeing statistics context and related releases.
ONS population and social-trends statistical context.

boundary: This record adds a repeated official wellbeing-and-salience layer: broad wellbeing, anxiety, loneliness, and public issue priorities are related but non-equivalent measures. It does not establish causality, clinical mental-health prevalence, actual consumer behavior, or the policy causes of age differences.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ONS dataset page and linked Excel workbook reviewed for August 2026 personal wellbeing, threshold, loneliness, trend, and important-issue tables.
reproduction_audit.version_note: ONS dataset page records a correction posted 7 September 2026 to July 2026 Table 24; this record uses the 5 to 30 August 2026 workbook and does not silently backfill the corrected historical table.
